tracks.title: Write a line, see the row
tracks.text: Lesson four point one — syntax. A deep dive, under org. You read the parent lesson… and you nodded along. Org is the written layer. Markdown can't see structure. Fine. But here's the problem — you still can't write org with confidence. And you don't know which lines of its twenty-year-old grammar this ecosystem actually honors. [curious] So this page is the receipt. Write a line… see the row. Every construct, drilled against the kernel's real output. Eight fields per headline — and that is the whole contract.

tracks.title: Folklore versus grammar
tracks.text: First — folklore versus grammar. Org-mode the Emacs thing is twenty years deep. Agenda views… footnotes… clock tables… capture templates. A folklore so large that no two org users have ever met who used the same tenth of it. [chuckles] Read its manual and you'll learn a hundred constructs. Read this ecosystem's parser… and you'll learn it honors maybe a dozen. That gap is the whole problem. A spec tells you what a feature is supposed to do. Specs are aspirational — and they lie by omission about what an implementation actually reads. The kernel here is not org-mode. It's an opinionated lens, pointed at org text, surfacing exactly the lines that carry meaning. So we won't learn grammar from a spec. We'll learn it from the parser itself. Write a line… run it through the kernel… read the JSON it hands back. A construct that produces a field is grammar. A construct that vanishes… is folklore. The parser is the only authority that never lies — because it's the thing the system actually runs.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Syntax, here, is the subset of org-mode the kernel surfaces as structure. Exactly eight fields per headline… plus a handful of section-level constructs. Everything else is prose — rendered, never parsed into meaning. The headline is the unit. Parse any file, and you get one row per headline, and every row has these eight keys, no more, no fewer. Let me name them. First, level — from the run of leading stars. Second, title — the headline text, with tags stripped off. Third, state — a leading TODO or DONE keyword, otherwise null. Fourth, tags — the trailing colon-run at the end of the line. Fifth, props — the properties drawer, with its keys uppercased. Sixth, id — sugar, the ID property lifted up to the top. Seventh, scheduled. And eighth, deadline — both of those, timestamps. Eight fields. That's the entire contract for a headline. And it's small enough to hold in your head precisely because the kernel is opinionated. [curious] The grammar isn't small by accident… it's small by design. So that what one human writes… another human, and every agent, read the exact same way.

tracks.title: The drill loop
tracks.text: Now — the drill loop. This is the method for the whole page, and the method you'll keep after it. Picture one line saved to a file — a TODO headline that says water the plants, tagged home — and you run wbx query on that file. And wbx query calls the kernel and prints the JSON rows. No project… no config… no setup. The kernel is a pure function from text… to rows. Picture the flow as a little machine with two stages inside it. On the left, org text goes in — one line, or a whole file. It enters the kernel. First stage — orgize parses the org tree. Second stage — and this is the one that matters — the lens. The lens walks that tree, keeps only the eight fields the system cares about, and lets everything else fall through as prose. Out the right side… come the JSON rows. [excited] And here's the promise. Every example past this point is real output from that function. Nothing is illustrative. Each one was machine-verified. You can reproduce any of them by saving the org to a file and running wbx query on it.

tracks.title: Anatomy of one line
tracks.text: Anatomy of one line. A headline is positional — read it left to right, and each region is a different field. Let me read you the fullest one a headline can carry. It starts with a single star — that's the stars, giving level one. Then the word TODO — that's the state keyword, and only TODO or DONE count. Then, in brackets, hash A — that's a priority cookie, and it gets silently swallowed. Then the words, rotate signing key — that's the title. And at the very end, colon ops colon security colon — that's the trailing tag run. All together, that one line parses to a row where level is one, state is TODO, title is just rotate signing key — clean, cookie gone — and tags is a list of two, ops and security. Now drill the edges, because that's where confidence is won or lost. [curious] First — a headline needs a star at column zero, and a space after it. A star jammed against text with no space… is not a headline, it vanishes entirely. An indented star… also gone. Column zero, then a space. Second — tags can't contain spaces. Colon ops colon security colon is two tags. But colon a-space-b colon… is not a tag at all — it stays in the title as literal text. And third — the priority cookie has no field. The hash-A is real org syntax, swallowed cleanly… but the kernel exposes no priority key anywhere. If you lean on priorities, the lens does not see them. An honest limit.

tracks.title: The one-line rule
tracks.text: The one-line rule. This is the single gotcha most likely to bite you — so it gets its own section. The planning line — the SCHEDULED and DEADLINE stamps — must sit on the one line directly under the headline. Together. Split them across two lines… and the parse quietly falls apart. And not just for the planning fields. Picture the same content two ways. In the broken way, you put SCHEDULED and DEADLINE on separate lines, with a properties drawer below. What comes back? Only scheduled parses. Deadline is null. And — this is the cruel part — the properties drawer right below silently stops being recognized. Your props come back as an empty object. In the fixed way, both stamps share one line, drawer below. What comes back? Both scheduled and deadline parse. The drawer parses. The ID lifts. Everything works. So here's the verdict of those two rows — the failure cascades. The second planning line poisons the drawer that comes after it. Your owner property… your ID… your whole record… evaporates to nothing, because of a stray newline two lines up. [sighs] And there's no error. The row just comes back hollow. So when a drawer mysteriously parses to nothing… this is the first place to look. One line. Always one line.

tracks.title: Headline as record
tracks.text: Headline as record. A properties drawer turns a headline into a typed record. Two rules carry most of the surprises. First rule — keys get uppercased. Write colon owner colon, space, shane… and in the JSON it comes back as OWNER, all caps, with the value trimmed. The key you read is never the key you typed, casing-wise. Second rule — the ID is special. Write colon I-D colon, rotate-key… and it appears twice. Once inside props, like every property. And once promoted to a top-level id field. Why twice? Because the system asks what is this headline's identity often enough to earn the shortcut. This section is deliberately short — the drawers deep dive takes the property mechanism all the way down… to toolkit manifests and agent identities.

tracks.title: The clock glyphs
tracks.text: The clock glyphs. A depth rung — skippable, and the timestamps deep dive goes the whole distance. But the shape is worth seeing once. The brackets decide everything. An angle-bracketed timestamp — twenty twenty-six, June twentieth, nine A-M, plus one week — parses to an object that says active, true. A square-bracketed one parses to active, false. So — angle brackets mean active, true. This is a thing the engine should act on. Square brackets mean active, false — a record of when something happened, inert. And the parser is loose by design. The date is just whichever token is ten characters long with a dash in the right spot. The time is the first token with a colon. The repeater is a token starting with plus, dot-plus, or plus-plus. Day names like Sat are skipped, never validated — write nonsense there and it shrugs. [chuckles] One honest leak to know now. A time range passes through raw. Nine A-M to ten-thirty… lands in the time slot whole, as a single string. The lens doesn't split it. It just hands you the string.

tracks.title: Blocks that compile
tracks.text: Blocks that compile. Another depth rung — the tangling deep dive is where this becomes a build system. The mechanic — a headline's section can carry a source block, and the kernel captures the first one only. Its language… its header args… its body. And the header-arg grammar is six keys. First, deps — a comma-split list. Second, uses. Third, in. Fourth, out. Fifth, persist — a bare flag. And sixth, dir. Anything else is silently ignored. Now the interesting part. Picture a small plan. A top headline called etl, tagged workflow, carrying a schedule property — cron, zero six star star star, every morning at six. Under it, two children, each tagged component. First child, fetch — a JavaScript block that uses http and outputs prices-dot-json. Second child, report — a Python block that depends on pandas, takes prices-dot-json in, outputs report-dot-html, and is marked persist. Run that through wbx tangle, and the kernel computes — nobody draws — a world. Picture it. Fetch and report sit inside the plan. Then an arrow, labelled prices-dot-json, runs from fetch to report. That edge was inferred — purely because fetch's out matched report's in. Off to the side, imports — http. And exports — report-dot-html, the output nobody consumed. The schedule rides along as cron. Two tagged headlines… and you have a scheduled, capability-aware build graph. [excited] Now watch this. Delete fetch… and run wbx lint. Back comes one error — level error, scope report — input prices-dot-json has no upstream producer. The validator flags exactly two kinds of error — a component with no source block, and an input with no producer. So that's a syntax error… that is also a plan error. Report wants an input that nothing makes. And that's the bridge to the workflows lessons — the same grammar that lists your to-dos… also type-checks your build.

tracks.title: The autopsy
tracks.text: The autopsy. The parent lesson argued that markdown can't see structure. Here's the receipt. Take that same rotate-key task… and write it the way a careful person writes markdown. A hash heading that says TODO rotate signing key. Then a sentence — bold Scheduled, the date, repeat weekly, tags ops and security. Everything a human needs, laid out clearly. Run it through the very same kernel. And what comes back… is an empty array. Zero rows. Not a degraded parse — nothing. [sighs] Every fact a human reads in that markdown — it's a task, it's a TODO, it's scheduled, it repeats, it's tagged — all of it is invisible to the machine. A hash heading is not a star headline. Bold text is not a state keyword. A prose sentence is not a property drawer. The information is all there, perfectly legible to you… and the parser sees an empty array. So here's the verdict. Org gives you one full row, eight typed fields. Markdown gives you nothing — an empty bracket pair. Same characters on the page. One of them, the kernel can answer questions about. That's the whole why-not-markdown argument… compressed into one command.

tracks.title: Dissect the easter egg
tracks.text: Dissect the easter egg. The parent page hides a comment in its own HTML source — a note for whoever views the page the honest way. And it isn't decoration. It's valid org, and it parses to a real row. Let me read you that row. The title — you found the written layer. The tags — easter, and egg. And a property — DISCOVERED — whose value reads, by viewing source, the honest way. The title's clean. The trailing colon-easter-colon-egg became the tags. And a colon-discovered property became DISCOVERED, all caps, in props — the same uppercasing rule from a moment ago, proving itself on a comment nobody was supposed to find. [mischievously] The lesson inside the lesson — org lives anywhere plain text lives. View-source on the parent is itself the drill. And… this page hides one too. Go look.

tracks.title: Where the lens stops
tracks.text: Where the lens stops. The honest part. The kernel is a lens, not org-mode — and a lens has edges. Knowing them is the difference between trusting the grammar… and being surprised by it. Let me walk the edges. First — custom TODO keywords. Words like WAIT or KILLED are not recognized. Only TODO and DONE. A config line declaring them is ignored, and star WAIT foo comes back with state null, the word WAIT just sitting in the title. Second — the priority cookie, hash-A. Swallowed from the title, exposed as no field. Third — time ranges pass through raw, into the time slot, as one string, not split. Fourth — the split planning line, which we drilled — only the first stamp parses, and it kills the drawer below. Fifth — a second source block in one section is ignored. Only the first is captured. Sixth — and this one's fun — the kernel's lint export is a stub that returns an empty array. The CLI's wbx lint doesn't call it. It calls validate — a different function, with real output. And the last edge is the honest summary of the whole page. Agenda views, links, footnotes, tables, clock tables — all of org's enormous surface still renders. The kernel's render is just orgize turning org into HTML, so all of it comes out as fine HTML. It just doesn't become structure the system computes on. The lens surfaces what the ecosystem needs machine-readable… and renders the rest as the document it is. That's not a missing feature. It's the line between structure and prose… drawn on purpose.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I add custom TODO keywords, like WAIT or BLOCKED? No — verified. Only TODO and DONE. A config line for them is ignored, and the word just stays in the title. If you need more states, they live in properties or tags. Where did my priority cookie go? Swallowed cleanly — your title comes back without it — but there's no priority field anywhere. Put it in a property instead. Is this all of org-mode? No — and that's the point. A lens over org, not the twenty-year feature set. A dozen-ish constructs carry meaning. The rest renders as prose. How do I check my own file? Run it through the kernel — wbx query, your file. You get the JSON rows back. If a field's missing or a drawer came back empty… you found a syntax issue. The parser is the spec. Does this run live in the browser? The machinery exists — a browser build with four exported functions, built for exactly this. An earlier in-page notebook shipped, and was retired the same day. So today, this page prints machine-verified static output instead. Every snippet is real. And last — why is wbx lint not the same as the kernel's lint? [chuckles] A fun wrinkle. The kernel's lint export is a stub that returns nothing. The CLI routes around it… and calls validate, which is real. So wbx lint works. It just takes the back door.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's syntax. The subset of org the kernel surfaces as structure — eight fields per headline, every one machine-verified, because the parser is the only spec that never lies. If it landed, you can now write org with confidence… and you know exactly which lines carry meaning. The way back up is short. This was a deep dive under org — lesson four — the grammar itself, and why a written layer earns its place. And from here, four siblings go further down — tangling, for the build plan; drawers, for the record mechanism; timestamps, for the full date grammar; and the kernel, for the one crate behind all three. Write a line… see the row. That was the whole method.
